claude.sample_unit: individual model assessments (45 vignettes x 10 models x 3 prompts x 10 repetitions)

links.outcome: Intertrial output variability of LLM triage advice across 10 repeated runs per prompt
links.effect: Median Fleiss kappa 0.766 (default), 0.717 (recognition-primed), 0.751 (data-frame); most frequent recommendation consistency 76.9%, 66.9%, 71.1%; variability similar across prompts.
links.quote: Intertrial reliability—that is, the frequency with which a vignette received the same advice from the same model across multiple trials—was comparable across all prompts, with median Fleiss κ values of 0.766 (IQR 0.706‐0.884) for the default prompt, 0.717 (IQR 0.681‐0.743) for the recognition-primed prompt, and 0.751 (IQR 0.725‐0.773) for the data-frame prompt ( Table 3 ).

links.outcome: Triage accuracy with structured reasoning prompt templates versus default prompt
links.effect: Overall accuracy 63.3% default vs 67.6% recognition-primed (OR 2.26) and 66.7% data-frame (OR 2.05); self-care accuracy 13.4% to 29.8% and 24.6%. GPT-5.2 showed no benefit.
links.quote: Both the recognition-primed prompt (OR 2.26, z =8.69; P <.001) and the data-frame prompt (OR 2.05, z =7.23; P <.001) significantly increased accuracy compared to the default prompt.

links.outcome: Emergency case recognition and over-triage/under-triage error direction in LLM triage
links.effect: Both emergency cases correctly identified 100% with default prompt, 98-99% with NDM prompts; 88% of errors were over-triage, 12% under-triage. Only 2 emergency cases; no safety conclusions.
links.quote: Across all 3 prompts, the models tended to recommend higher-than-necessary urgency (accounting for 88% of all errors, 95% CI 87%‐88.9%) rather than lower-than-necessary urgency (12% of all errors, 95% CI 11.1%‐13%).

links.outcome: LLM care-seeking advice accuracy against physician-panel gold standard
links.effect: Overall accuracy with default prompt was 63.3% (95% CI 61.9%-64.7%); self-care accuracy only 13.4% with default prompt.
links.quote: The average accuracy across all models, vignettes, and trials was 63.3% (95% CI 61.9%‐64.7%) for the default prompt, 67.6% (95% CI 66.3%‐69%) for the recognition-primed prompt, and 66.7% (95% CI 65.3%‐68%) for the data-frame prompt.

links.effect: Higher-than-necessary urgency accounted for 88% of errors (95% CI 87%‐88.9%); lower-than-necessary urgency 12% (11.1%‐13%).
links.quote: Across all 3 prompts, the models tended to recommend higher-than-necessary urgency (accounting for 88% of all errors, 95% CI 87%‐88.9%) rather than lower-than-necessary urgency (12% of all errors, 95% CI 11.1%‐13%).

links.effect: Median Fleiss κ was 0.766 default, 0.717 recognition-primed, and 0.751 data-frame.
links.quote: Intertrial reliability—that is, the frequency with which a vignette received the same advice from the same model across multiple trials—was comparable across all prompts, with median Fleiss κ values of 0.766 (IQR 0.706‐0.884) for the default prompt, 0.717 (IQR 0.681‐0.743) for the recognition-primed prompt, and 0.751 (IQR 0.725‐0.773) for the data-frame prompt ( Table 3 ).

links.effect: GPT-5.2 self-care accuracy dropped to 0% in both Instant and Thinking and remained unchanged with NDM-inspired prompts.
links.quote: The benefits of using NDM-inspired prompts were replicated for GPT-5.1 (for both the Instant version without a reasoning process and the Thinking version with a reasoning process), but not for GPT-5.2: self-care accuracy dropped to 0% in both GPT-5.2 Instant and GPT-5.2 Thinking and remained unchanged with NDM-inspired prompts.
